title: CBT for IBS: How Clinicians Can Address Catastrophizing
summary: Brief CBT for IBS can ease catastrophizing in a routine visit. Learn 3 steps any clinician can use, when to refer, and where gut-brain therapy fits.
body_markdown:
Brief CBT for IBS lets clinicians address catastrophizing in a routine visit, new guidance shows, while an estimated 46% of US adults live over 25 miles from in-person GI psychology care.¹ ² When a referral means a long wait, your next visit may be the best chance to interrupt that thinking.


You’ll hear it in almost every clinic: “I’ll never get better,” or “this pain is going to ruin my whole day.”[New guidance](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12964511/) in the *Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition* makes the case that you don’t need to hand that thinking off to a referral and hope for the best.¹


Instead, it sets out a short framework drawn from cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) that fits inside a normal visit. It was written for pediatric gastroenterologists, but the skills aren’t specific to one specialty or age group: GI advanced practice providers (APPs), dietitians, primary care clinicians, and nurses hear the same thoughts, and gut-focused CBT uses the same skills with adults.


The authors are also clear it isn’t a call for clinicians to deliver ongoing CBT themselves.¹


## What cognitive distortions look like in IBS and gut-brain disorders


Cognitive distortions are automatic, biased thoughts that reinforce negative thinking, and in gut-brain disorders they tend to center on what a symptom means and what will happen next.¹ Catastrophizing, or jumping to the worst possible outcome, is the most familiar.


They matter clinically because fear of future GI symptoms, known as GI-specific visceral anxiety, is linked to symptom exacerbation, lower quality of life, and more anxiety and depression.¹ Helplessness about pain has been linked to greater GI symptoms, distress, and disability too.¹


> “Gut symptoms are not just relayed from the periphery or from the organ. They’re shaped and filtered by the brain.”
>
>
> –[Dr. Dany Lamothe](https://www.nervahealth.com/article/emotions-gut-symptoms-ibs) , Medical Psychiatrist, Stanford University School of Medicine⁴


These are the 3 distortions the guidance highlights, with the kind of response it suggests:¹


Cognitive distortion What you might hear A response to try


Catastrophizing “I’ll never get better.” “I see a lot of patients with this, and many improve a great deal. What makes you sure you won’t?”


Fortune telling “This new medication won’t work either.” “Can you remember a time you felt better? What was different then?”


Overgeneralization “I can’t live a normal life.” “What’s the evidence for that, and what’s the evidence against it?”


Targeting these thoughts is the core of gut-focused CBT, which has one of the strongest evidence bases among psychological therapies for IBS in a[network meta-analysis of 41 trials](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32276950/) .³


The good news is that the first steps don’t require a therapist.


##
3 brief CBT steps to address catastrophizing in a clinic visit


Clinicians can address catastrophizing in 3 steps during routine care: explain what a cognitive distortion is, help the patient label it, then question or reframe it.¹ The guidance frames them for gastroenterologists, but they fit just as well in a dietitian consult or a primary care visit, and you can spread them across appointments.


### Step 1: Explain catastrophizing with brief psychoeducation


Brief psychoeducation means naming the thought trap when you hear it, and explaining why it matters. When a patient says their new medication won’t help and surgery is inevitable, you might reflect that their mind is jumping to the worst outcome, which is common when people feel unwell, and that these thought errors can make symptoms feel worse.¹


It helps to be clear that naming a thought doesn’t mean the symptoms aren’t real. Our guide to[explaining IBS as a real disorder of gut-brain interaction](https://www.nervahealth.com/article/ibs-misinformation-social-media-clinicians) covers that framing.


### Step 2: Help patients recognize and label cognitive distortions


Labeling turns a passing thought into something the patient can spot on their own. When a patient says their symptoms are never going away, pause and ask what kind of thought that might be, and how it could affect their pain.¹


Model it first, then hand it over. Over time, patients and families can start catching these thoughts in real time, between visits.¹


### Step 3: Question the evidence or reframe the thought


Once a thought is labeled, patients can either test it or rewrite it.¹ To test it, ask: “What evidence do you have that this is true, and what evidence says it isn’t?” A simpler version is “Is this thought helpful?”


To reframe, help the patient soften the thought rather than replace it with forced positivity. “My pain is going to ruin my day” becomes “I’m worried my pain will ruin my day, but I have skills to manage it.”¹


### Applying this in practice


Pick one step per visit rather than trying all 3 at once. Listen for “never,” “always,” and “ruin” in how patients describe their symptoms, and use that moment to name the pattern.


For dietitians, catastrophizing often shows up around food: “If I eat onion, my whole week is ruined.” The same question-the-evidence step works there, and it can help when fear, rather than symptoms, is driving restriction.


If the thinking doesn’t shift, or it’s clearly driving how the patient functions, that’s your cue to refer.

## When to refer to a GI psychologist for catastrophizing or GI-specific anxiety


GI psychology referral is the right next step when brief in-visit work isn’t enough, and the guidance names three groups who need it.¹ These micro-interventions are meant to start the work, not replace specialist care.


### Who to refer to GI psychology


-


Patients with high levels of distress or functional impairment


-


Patients with chronic GI symptoms


-


Patients with psychological comorbidities, such as anxiety or depression¹


### When a GI psychologist isn’t available


The Rome Foundation’s GastroPsych directory is the place to start, and the guidance suggests a general behavioral health clinician if no GI psychologist is available.¹


That’s a common problem. Adults with bowel DGBIs were no more likely to have been offered CBT than people without GI disease in a 2026 survey, even though those with other GI diseases had 4.3 times the odds.⁵ And an analysis we undertook at Nerva estimated that that 16 states have no listed in-person GI psychology specialist at all.²


##
Using brief CBT techniques with children, teens, and their parents


Brief CBT techniques work well with children and teens when you bring parents in as coaches. The guidance suggests modeling the skills in clinic so caregivers can support their child to use them at home, at school, and in the community.¹


Guidelines back the approach. The joint European and North American Societies for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN and NASPGHAN) 2025 guideline for IBS and functional abdominal pain in children aged 4 to 18 includes gut-brain psychotherapies such as CBT and gut-directed hypnotherapy.⁶ Our article on[pediatric IBS guidelines and gut-directed hypnotherapy](https://www.nervahealth.com/article/pediatric-ibs-guidelines-hypnotherapy) covers what changed.


How you frame it for families matters as much as the technique:


> “I always make it really clear early on: this is not all in your head, and it’s not all anxiety. What’s happening in your head, your thoughts and experiences, does influence what’s happening in your gut. But you can often feel a weight lift off the child and their parents’ shoulders when you say that.”
>
>
> – Dr. Charmaine Chai, Pediatric Gastroenterologist (Neurogastroenterology & Motility), Women’s and Children’s Hospital, Adelaide


### Watch: Managing pediatric patients with gut-brain disorders, with Harvard GI Dr. Mark Salvatore


Watch Harvard pediatric gastroenterologist Dr. Mark Salvatore, Founding Clinical Director of the Pediatric Mind-Body Medicine Program at Mass General Brigham for Children, talk through the gut-brain axis and how he manages pediatric patients with gut-brain disorders.


## Where gut-brain therapy fits when a GI psychologist isn’t available


Gut-brain therapy gives patients a structured way to keep working on the gut-brain connection between visits, especially when specialist care is out of reach. The American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) guideline suggests gut-directed psychotherapy for global IBS symptoms.⁷ A Rome Foundation working team also recommends brain-gut behavior therapies across disorders of gut-brain interaction.⁸


Nerva is a digital gut-brain therapy program patients access via a phone app. It combines gut-directed hypnotherapy with CBT-informed education and breathing exercises, so it reinforces the same skills you start in clinic, in 15–20 minutes a day.


In a randomized controlled trial of 244 adults with IBS, 81% of Nerva participants achieved a clinically meaningful improvement on the IBS Symptom Severity Scale, compared with 63% on an active control.⁹


You can[refer](https://www.nervahealth.com/eu/article/clinician-resource-referring-patients-nerva) patients through the clinician form or simply recommend Nerva.


## Frequently asked questions


### How does CBT treat IBS?


CBT treats IBS by changing the thoughts and behaviors, such as catastrophizing, symptom-checking, and avoidance, that amplify gut symptoms.¹ It’s one of 5 main brain-gut behavior therapies identified by a Rome Foundation working team, usually delivered over a short course of sessions.⁸


### Is catastrophizing a mental illness?


Catastrophizing is a thinking pattern, not a mental illness or diagnosis in itself: it’s a type of cognitive distortion that tends to increase distress.¹ It often travels with anxiety and depression, which is why persistent, impairing catastrophizing is a reason to refer to GI psychology.¹


### Is there an app for CBT for IBS?


Self-guided and minimal-contact CBT for IBS has trial support, and in a network meta-analysis it was about as efficacious as face-to-face CBT.³ Digital gut-brain therapy programs such as Nerva combine CBT-informed education with gut-directed hypnotherapy.


### How do you refer a patient to a digital gut-brain therapy program?


A referral to Nerva can be made through the clinician form or by recommending the program in a consult. Referrals don’t expire, so patients can start when they feel ready.
